title: XSkill: Continual Learning from Experience and Skills in Multimodal Agents
one_liner: XSkill lets a multimodal agent keep improving from past runs by storing both short action guidance and larger reusable skills, each tied to what the agent actually saw.
lead: A multimodal agent often faces two kinds of repeated knowledge. One kind is local: on this kind of screen or image, this next action usually helps because a similar visual cue has already signaled the same next move before. The other kind is procedural: for this kind of task, these steps in this order usually work. XSkill stores both. It extracts concise experiences for local guidance and broader skills for task-level guidance, then retrieves them using the current visual observation so that past knowledge stays connected to the situation that needs it.

problem.h2: Why multimodal agents waste past experience
paras: A multimodal agent may solve many tasks and still fail to improve much from them. One reason is that past runs are stored as raw histories without being turned into guidance that can be reused. Another reason is that retrieval often ignores the current visual scene, so the agent pulls back advice that matched the old text but not the old observation.

XSkill treats continual improvement as a storage-and-retrieval design problem. It asks what kind of knowledge should be stored, how it should be tied to visual evidence, and how it should be brought back when a new observation resembles an old one.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Store two streams of reusable knowledge, short experiences and larger skills, tie both to visual observations, and feed later usage back into the storage loop so that the agent keeps learning from its own history.

panels.title: 1. The agent sees and acts
panels.viz_args: image or screen + tools + action history
panels.caption: A multimodal task produces both visual evidence and action decisions.

panels.title: 2. Two kinds of knowledge are extracted
panels.caption: One stream stores local experience and the other stores broader skills because the agent needs both kinds of reuse.

panels.title: 3. Visual grounding stays attached
panels.viz_args: knowledge linked to what was seen
panels.caption: Each stored item remains tied to the relevant observation so that later retrieval can match the real scene.

panels.title: 4. New tasks retrieve both streams
panels.viz_args: current view -> fetch experiences and skills
panels.caption: The current observation pulls back local hints and broader procedures that fit it.

panels.title: 5. Usage feeds the next round
panels.caption: What worked this time goes back into accumulation, so continual learning keeps moving.

steps.text: Collect several attempts on the same task so that the system can compare weak and strong behavior.
Extract short experiences for local action guidance and larger skills for task-level guidance.

steps.b: Step 3: Tie them to visual observations
steps.text: Store each item with the relevant visual context because later retrieval should depend on what the agent is actually seeing.

steps.b: Step 4: Retrieve and adapt during later tasks
steps.text: Bring back the most relevant experience and skill items when a new task observation matches them.

steps.b: Step 5: Feed usage back into storage
steps.text: Use later success and failure signals to refine what stays in memory, so that continual learning does not stop after one round.

paras: The paper changes both the form of memory and the learning loop around it. It stores two reusable knowledge streams and reconnects later usage back to accumulation.

hidden.name: how well a stored experience or skill matches the current visual situation that triggers retrieval
paras: The hidden quantity is observation-knowledge fit. A stored hint only helps if it matches what the agent is seeing now, because otherwise retrieval becomes generic and the wrong past advice returns.

XSkill improves this fit by grounding both experiences and skills in visual observations and by updating memory from later usage. That matters because continual learning is only useful when the right past knowledge comes back in the right current scene.

heat.caption: Dark cells mark stored knowledge that matches the current observation closely enough to guide the next action or the broader plan.

reads.html: The stored advice has to fit what the agent is looking at right now, because otherwise the memory will return guidance for the wrong scene.
XSkill improves multimodal continual learning by grounding both action-level experience and task-level skill memory in visual observations, so retrieval stays situation-aware.

paras: The two-stream design matters because one memory type cannot do every job well. Short experiences are good for local moves such as what to click or inspect next. Larger skills are good for preserving the broader procedure across a full task.

Visual grounding matters because multimodal tasks are scene-dependent. The same text instruction can require different actions on different screens or images. By tying memory to what was seen, XSkill improves retrieval precision when the agent faces a similar observation later.

The continual loop matters because memory quality should evolve. Later usage reveals which stored items remain helpful and which should be revised or dropped, so the system gets better by reusing its own history rather than by only collecting more raw episodes.

stages.s: extract short experiences and larger skills
ground both in the relevant observations
retrieve and adapt during later tasks
agent that keeps improving from its own history

math.words: Keep experiences and skills that match the current observation well and that improve later task success when reused.
math.equation: J = E[ reuse_gain(E_t, S_t | obs_t) - alpha * mismatch_cost - beta * stale_memory_cost ]
symbols: the retrieved experience items at task step t
the retrieved skill items at task step t
the current visual observation and task state
improvement from using the retrieved experience and skill items in the current situation
penalty when retrieved items do not fit the current observation
penalty for keeping old items that no longer help later tasks

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: A web navigation agent has solved several checkout tasks before.
On a new page, the current observation shows a shipping form that matches one stored local experience and one stored checkout skill.
The experience says where the delivery option usually appears, and the skill says the broader order of steps for finishing checkout.
Together they shorten the search and avoid a wrong detour, so reuse gain is high.
If an old memory points to a page layout that no longer matches, it raises mismatch cost and should be revised or removed later.

math.note: This compact objective captures the paper's main point: stored knowledge is valuable when it matches the current visual situation, because matched retrieval can guide the current step and still support later tasks.

charts.title: Tool-only or single-memory baselines
charts.note: These baselines leave reuse value on the table because they either store no reusable knowledge or store only one type of guidance.

charts.title: XSkill
charts.note: XSkill improves these outcomes because local experience and broader skills complement each other and both stay grounded in what the agent sees.

items.html: If a stored item is linked to a vague observation, later retrieval may return it in the wrong scene because the visual match is too weak.

items.b: The two streams duplicate each other.
items.html: If experiences and skills store nearly the same content, memory becomes bloated because the split is no longer helping different levels of guidance.
A stale item can keep hurting later tasks because continual learning keeps reusing advice that no longer matches new environments.
The approach works when observation grounding is precise and later usage updates the memory store, because then the right local hint and the right broader skill come back together.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small multimodal benchmark with repeated web or desktop tasks where each task includes both visual state and tool actions. Let one agent store only raw histories. Let another extract observation-grounded experiences and skills, retrieve them on later tasks, and update the memory store after reuse. Include a few changed layouts so that visual grounding matters.

The demo should show better transfer and lower task time for the dual-stream agent because the right local hint and the right broader procedure are both available when the current scene matches past work.
demo.metric_eq: reuse_success = helpful_retrievals / total_retrievals ; transfer_gain = solved_after_memory - solved_without_memory
demo.closing: The decisive evidence is that grounded dual-stream memory improves later tasks, because both local guidance and broader procedure are retrieved in the scenes where they actually fit.
